# The Month-End Close Checklist for Firms Closing Many Books at Once

Every month end close checklist you can find online was written for one company closing one set of books. Yours is not that. You are two people closing thirty client books inside the same nine days, and the thing that makes that hard was never the steps.

## Why the standard month end close checklist breaks in a practice

The twelve-step list is fine. Reconcile the bank, post the accruals, review payroll, close the subledgers, produce the statements. Nobody in a practice is confused about what to do.

What goes wrong is the order. Left alone, a small firm closes clients in the order their documents arrive, which means the clients who send everything on the first working day get closed while there is still time to think, and the three who send nothing until the seventh get closed at speed on the eighth. The quality of your close ends up decided by your clients' filing habits.

## Sequence clients before you sequence tasks

Sort your clients on two axes before the window opens: how long their close takes when it goes well, and how likely they are to be late.

Run the short and reliable ones first. They clear quickly, they free the window, and finishing four books on day two changes how the rest of the month feels. Save the long and unreliable ones for the middle, never the end, because a client who is both slow and late needs slack behind them.

The client who is fast but always late is the one people get wrong. Do not put them last. Put them early with a hard chase on day one, because their close is short enough to absorb a two-day delay and nothing else in your window is.

## The nine steps, compressed

Everyone else writes three thousand words on these. Here they are in one line each, with the part that actually bites in a practice.

- **Reconcile bank and card accounts.** The failure is a broken feed you do not notice until day six.
- **Post accruals and prepayments.** The failure is carrying last month's schedule forward without reading it.
- **Review payroll.** The failure is a mid-month starter nobody told you about.
- **Close the subledgers.** The failure is an AR ledger the client is still posting into.
- **Produce and review the statements.** The failure is reviewing your own work at 6pm on the last day.

## What to do when three clients are missing documents at once

You have three moves and they are not equal.

**Chase** when the missing item is small, singular, and the client has answered you this month. Give it one round and a deadline.

**Estimate and accrue** when the item is predictable from history and the amount is immaterial to the statements. Write down that you estimated it and what you based it on. This is the move people skip because it feels like cheating, and it is the right move more often than they think.

**Move the client** when the missing item is structural, like an unreconciled year of a second bank account. Closing around it produces a set of statements you will have to redo. Tell the client that day, not on the deadline.

## How long a close should take, by firm size

Across 900 firms on Ledgerline, the median two-person practice takes 7.4 working days to close its book of clients. The top quartile takes 4.9. The difference is almost never software.

It is that the fast firms decided their client order before the window opened, and the slow ones decided it every morning.

## The parts you can safely automate

Rule-based reconciliation is safe on high-volume, low-variance accounts: card feeds, payment processors, payroll clearing. Let it run and review the exceptions.

It is not safe on intercompany accounts, on anything where the client posts manual journals, or in the first two months of a new client, when you do not yet know what normal looks like for them. Automating those does not save time. It moves the error to a place you will find it in month four.

## The handover note that saves you two hours

At the end of each client's close, write four lines. What you estimated and why. What is unreconciled and by how much. What the client still owes you. What you would do differently next month.

That note is the entire difference between a colleague picking up a client cold and a colleague booking two hours of your time to ask.
